en: Oṃ. (Then enters Mālyavān, dejected. Mālyavān:
(Reflecting) Alas! The sprouts of the tree of the Lord of Rākṣasas’ misconduct seem to have been scattered everywhere:
the seed was the daughter of the King of Videha; the sprout was the journey of his sister; the bud was the deceptive artifice of Mārīca;

the network of branches was the abduction of the one not born from a womb; its blossoms were clearly the slaying of the Lord of Monkeys and the departure of his younger brother; and the fruit is their alliance with him. (1)
I believe that this [plan] will soon bear fruit, for one of mature intellect perceives the future. (Sighing) Alas, the perversity of fate!
Whatever I have countered in this calamity through the power of counsel—
Just as the task of Alasa was performed by him, so too was each respective duty carried out by himself.
(With remorse: That which is called "assistance" leads to great anguish.
Whatever the arrogant do according to their own will and without restraint, a remedy for each such act must be devised, even when fate is adverse. (3)
Oh, how extraordinary is the conduct of that wicked Kṣatriya youth! What indeed has he not accomplished by gradually subduing the emperor of monkeys, who possesses such heat of valor?
(Acting as if remembering: And it was said by the spy who returned from Kiṣkindhā that the foremost of monkeys have been dispatched in every direction to search for Sītā.
(Offstage:

The mature fire, creating confusion for the seven surrounding oceans with its circles of ruddy rays whose expansion is unperceived within the walls of the eastern cities, and possessing a mass of gold intensely heated, devours Laṅkā—where the night-stalking warriors, half-burnt, are retreating while raising intense fears of the end of the world—as well as the crumbling Trikūṭa mountain. (4)
(Entering with a sudden toss of the curtain, Trijaṭā, in a state of agitation: "Save me! Save me, my younger maternal grandfather!"
(Thus he falls, beating his breast. Mālyavān: Child, enough of this timidity! What is this great calamity that has occurred?

Trijatā: (Rising) Youngest grandfather, what can I say, unfortunate as I am? Some wicked monkey indeed, having burnt the entire city in a mere moment—scattering the various Rākṣasa folk with the thrusts of his sharp claws—was pursued by Prince Akṣa; yet, having performed his sport there, he has suddenly departed.
Mālyavān: (With distress) What, has the city been burnt? Is Prince Akṣa slain? And who might this monkey be? (Recalling) Cāraka said that Hanūmat went toward the southern direction. Alas!
By Hanumān himself, while burning the city of Laṅkā as if it were a heap of cotton,
even the fierce majesty of the Lord of Laṅkā was extinguished.
My child, has he also obtained news concerning Sītā?

Trijatā: Just before my youngest grandfather, a certain monkey-creature was seen conversing with her. She too, having unfastened her hair-ornament, presented it as a token of recognition into his hand. This much I know.

Mālyavān: Is this not sufficient? (With apprehension) By a single atom of a monkey, such a feat has been accomplished. Now, it is heard that there are more than hundreds of millions in the race of monkeys protected by the strength of Sugrīva’s arms.
Trijatā:
(Reflecting) How is it that Sītā—though possessing such a delicate appearance, though accustomed to very tender food, and though being a human—has become a Rākṣasī even for us Rākṣasas?
Mālyavān: My child, it is indeed fitting;
she is proclaimed as a light consisting of devotion to her husband, one that is both tranquil and radiant.
(Reflecting: Or rather, what of her? She is but a poor thing.
This ripening of evil deeds blazes forth for those very individuals themselves. //6//

Trijatā: Youngest grandfather, our dwelling in various mountain regions situated on the borders of the Daṇḍaka forest was indeed our domain throughout the entire Jambūdvīpa. Now, even residence here in this city is unbearable. What is the way out? What is the remedy?
Mālyavān: Child, why are you so exceedingly despondent? Behold:
this Trikūṭa is difficult to traverse, and upon it stands the city with its sevenfold ramparts and walls; and this ocean, with its cloud-scraping waves, is an endless moat impossible to cross.
(Reflecting: Or rather, what is the use of this?
The very staff-like arms of the Lord of the Rākṣasas, which await the initiation for the great sacrifice of crushing the arrogant enemies— (indicating the throbbing of his left eye,
with distress) what is this ill-fated destiny that is powerless even to grant us a word? (7)
Child, how much remains until the end of Kumbhakarṇa’s sleep?
Trijatā: My youngest grandfather, on this very day of the fourteenth of the dark fortnight, the fourth month has come to an end.
Mālyavān: How is it that even now the time for awakening is said to be so very distant?

(Reflecting. But upon reflection, by good fortune, it is indeed my younger nephew who is far-sighted, whose impulsive actions even lead to auspicious results. No matter how many times I deliberate, I perceive him alone as the thread that sustains the lineage.
Trijatā: (With agitation) Youngest grandfather! Alas, alas! May sin be stilled; may this inauspiciousness be averted!
Mālyavān: Why so?
Trijaṭā: This report concerning my youngest maternal uncle has been directed toward someone else entirely, and toward something most inauspicious indeed.

Mālyavān: Child, that was not said with reference to him. It is rather understood thus: for this path of pure policy does not fall anywhere else, nor does the intellect of its traveler, except by the power of an irresistible destiny.
Just as the sun, wandering freely and boundlessly through the sky, casts aside the peak of the setting mountain, and so too does that ray of the day follow it.
Therefore, regarding these remedies, nothing remains but the employment of stratagems; this has already been done. My child, do you know what the first step of the ten-necked Rāvaṇa’s plan is?

Trijaṭā: My dear youngest grandfather, my lord has now ascended the watchtower named Sarvatobhadra and remains gazing only toward that Aśoka grove presided over by that night which is the dark destroyer of the Rākṣasa race. Moreover, this news was heard from her who set out in this direction: having experienced some distress upon hearing these events in the city, the lady has set out for that very place to awaken the King.

Mālyavān: Child, even in her state as a woman, that Queen Mandodarī is indeed superior, for her mind still exerts itself to awaken him; not so the King, who, though awakened even now, does not yet understand. Therefore, come, let us enter the inner apartments and deliberate upon our secret mission.
(Thus they both exit. //The Interlude//

(Then enters Rāvaṇa, full of longing. Rāvaṇa: (Beholding Sītā: If her face is present, what need is there for the moon? If her tremulous eyes are there, what need for clusters of blue lotuses? If the undulating play of her eyebrows exists, what need for ripples on the water?

What is the use of the bow of the Self-born (Brahmā) if her locks of hair are so well-restrained? What is the use of the grandeur of the clouds if this body [is so radiant]? What is the use of Śrī (the Goddess of Fortune)? //9//
(With the joy of remembrance: Ah! My desire, which has been pursuing the jewel among women manifested from the earth split open by the plowshare, has finally borne fruit after a long time.
(Reflecting: This is surely the play of a favorable destiny.
(Proudly: Or rather, who is this so-called "destiny" anyway?

If, having ground this universe and cast aside even some of its divisions of worlds, and having appointed Brahmā as my representative while assuming for myself my own incomparable mass of splendor, majesty, and fame—having established the sun and moon—I myself were to become exceedingly content, it would not be the fault of indolence; or rather, how could there be anger toward those who are objects of compassion? (10)
(Then enter Mandodarī and a maidservant. Maidservant: This way, this way, mistress! Here is the door to the staircase of the watchtower; please ascend, mistress.
Mandodarī: (Acting out the act of ascending the stairs; observing Rāvaṇa) Why, here is the Great King Daśakaṇṭha sitting!
(Gazing closely) Why, he is looking toward the Aśoka grove!
(With distress: How is it that even now, despite such an occasion for displaying his prowess having arrived, the Great King Dashagriva appears indifferent to the affairs of state?
(Approaching: Victory, victory to the Great King Dashagriva!
Rāvaṇa: (Acting out the concealment of his expression) What, Mandodarī?
(He seats her by his side.)
Mandodarī:
(Having done so) Great King, what is there to be thought about here?
Rāvaṇa: Where?
Mandodarī: [She speaks] with a face like that of a lioness.
Rāvaṇa:
(With a sneer) How is it that the Queen is being told things she has never heard before—of an enemy, his faction, and an attack upon him?

As for me, who with my two arms simultaneously blocked the tusks of the rutting elephants of the quarters on the field of battle, and with my four arms forcibly restrained even the guardians of the directions as they fell upon me!
My chest-skin has been crushed by the falling of fierce weapons, such as blazing vajras; yet that he considers himself my rival—this is some unprecedented delusion on his part. //11//
Very well; nevertheless, it must be heard. O Queen, who is he?
Mandodarī: It is heard that the son of Daśaratha, Rāma—the leader of the host of Sugrīva, who is followed by the entire circle of monkeys—has arrived here with his younger brother.
Rāvaṇa: Is that ascetic accompanied by his younger brothers? My Queen, what does it matter to me about him or them?

Mandodarī: Great King, it is indeed said that there was a general commotion. Moreover, having stationed his army at the shores of the Sāgara, he challenged the ocean, yet the ocean did not emerge from its abode. At that time—(resorting to Sanskrit)—he discharged a certain weapon into the depths of the ocean, by the power of which the entire water, boiling for half a moment, turned red and whirled about like a potter’s wheel.

Suddenly, the circle of crocodiles was uprooted, the multitude of turtles was shattered, the humans in the water were utterly bewildered, an incomparable roar resounded, and the conch shells and oysters were tossed about.
Rāvaṇa:
(With contempt) And what of it?

Mandodarī: Great King, furthermore, after the ocean—its body bristling from the volley of sharp arrows whose feathers alone were visible—had emerged from the waters and offered the path by promising the slaughter of Rāvaṇa, it was heard that he [Rāvaṇa] was being urged on by that reckless one.
Rāvaṇa: (Laughing) Let it be; it is heard. O Queen, what is it like?
Mandodarī: Great King, the bridge is being constructed by mountain peaks brought by thousands of monkeys led by Valīmukha.
Rāvaṇa: O Queen, you have been deceived by someone. This Lord of the Waters is indeed one whose greatness of depth has not been fathomed. Behold:
however many mountains there may be in Jambūdvīpa or even in other continents, they do not fill even a corner of his belly. (13)

Moreover, while the Queen says "by that rash act," there is another person in this world who has almost forgotten what rashness is. As for my own rash deed, however, Śiva is the authority—he whose feet were honored by the lotus-like face of the Goddess, which possessed the manifest beauty of a smile as sweet as abundant tears of joy, and whose feet were washed by the returning streams of fresh blood flowing clearly from the bursting veins of her throbbing neck. 14.
Mandodarī: Great King, take heart; those mountain peaks remain in the water quite differently from any other jewel, for they stay even above the reach of the touch of any monkey's hand.
Rāvaṇa:
(With a shake of his head) This is that irresistible naiveté of women, by which even stones float! O Queen, what is the use of saying more?
I have heard that my companion Śrutikavi knows the command of Indra, that the thunderbolt is the comrade of Śacī, and that this world of three realms is the fame of the mountain.
The strength [of this act] was Mount Kailāsa; what other audacity, alas, could there be, than that the wielder of the broken-axe (Śiva) had his feet bathed by the flowing nectar-water? //15//
(A great clamor behind the scenes. Mandodarī: Great King, save me, save me! (She looks on in terror.)
Rāvaṇa: My lady, enough with this apprehension.

(Again, behind the scenes: O you Rākṣasas guarding the gates of Laṅkā! Quickly open the gates and cast upon them bolts made of solid stone as heavy as Sāla trees; bring that collection of weapons and place it over them, and take heed of both yourselves and your enemies! Block those who wish to flee, and protect the children, women, and the transport of supplies! Rāmabhadra has arrived, accompanied by his younger brothers and surrounded by a host of monkeys led by Sugrīva. (16)
(From behind the scenes, a female door-keeper enters halfway: "My Lord, the commander-in-chief stands at the entrance, desiring to make a representation."
Rāvaṇa: What, is it the commander-in-chief Prahasta? Let him enter.
Portress: Very well. (She exits.
(Then Prahasta enters.)
Prahasta: Oh, how exceedingly powerful is the conduct of this mere human child! For instance:
having leaped as easily as over a cow’s footprint across the terrifying Lord of Waters, who is filled on all sides with garlands of waves, he has approached Laṅkā with eyes fixed upon it;
and having established his camp upon the rugged summit of Mount Suvela, he himself, surrounded by certain preeminent monkeys, occupies the front courtyard. (17)
(Looking ahead: What, is this the Lord of Laṅkā?
(Approaching: Victory, victory to the Lord of Laṅkā!
Rāvaṇa: My good general, what is the cause of this clamor?
Prahasta:
(To himself) How is it that even now His Majesty remains ignorant? Very well; I shall inform him of the matter alone.
(Aloud)
The city had its gates and doors completely closed and was surrounded on all sides by trusted and devoted Rākṣasas who stood as guards. //18//
Rāvaṇa: What is it?
Prahasta: (To himself) How is it that the situation is exactly the same? Very well.
(Aloud) O Lord, Lord of Laṅkā!
Today, by you and your younger brother, who are merely human children, your city is besieged such that even provisions and supplies are difficult to obtain. (19)
(Entering, the female door-keeper: My Lord, here is a certain monkey-faced man standing at the entrance of the portico, saying that he is a messenger from Rāma.
Rāvaṇa:
(With contempt) Valīmukha, let him enter!
Doorkeeper:
Very well. (Having exited and re-entering with Aṅgada; to him) Here is the Lord. Approach.
Aṅgada:
(Approaching) Victory, victory to the Lord of Laṅkā, the supreme devotee of Maheśvara!
Rāvaṇa: You are a follower of Sugrīva.
Aṅgada: No, no!
Rāvaṇa: In that case, to whom [does it belong]?
Aṅgada: O Lord of Laṅkā, hear who I am and for what purpose I have come.
By the command of that great forest-fire to the grove of the haughty Rākṣasa host, the messenger of the son of Daśaratha has come to you with his word to punish you.
Release Sītā; being joined by your kinsmen, friends, heirs, and sons, honor the feet of the son of Sumitrā; otherwise, O arrogant one, you shall be punished by his arrows.
Rāvaṇa: (With a laugh) Even Valīmukha is talkative! What more need be said?

Aṅgada: Let me be whatever I may be; you, however, must simply determine the final conclusion. Tell me, which of these two do you prefer: those who bow their heads to touch His lotus-feet and toenails, or those who bow their heads to touch the tips of His sharp arrows? (21)
Rāvaṇa: (With anger) Ho there! Who is present here? Let someone polish the mouth of this fellow who speaks such nonsense!
Prahasta: Your Majesty, this is surely a messenger; what is the use of anger in this matter?
Rāvaṇa: This very refinement of his face is the ascetic’s reply.
Aṅgada:

(Gesticulating the throbbing of his hair-pores) By means of those [hands] whose tendons have been loosened by the forceful action of sharp saws and cruel, jagged claws, acting in their respective order...
If I were not subject to another due to my role as a messenger for the Lord of the Raghus, how could I return without having brought back Vali from all directions upon the crowns of your heads? 22.
(Thus leaping away, he exits. Rāvaṇa:
(Observing. Oh, how this fickleness, so natural to one's birth, is beyond remedy!
Prahasta: My Lord, my heart yearns to receive the garland of letters that constitutes your command.
Rāvaṇa: What need is there even here to ask for instructions?
Let the bolts on all sides be shattered by the Rākṣasas, who are haughty with their world-renowned strength; let the spokes be split apart on every side by those intent on distracting the enemy.
Let my arms be adorned with the very ornaments of weapons that devour the foe, and let the monkeys—who are arrogant in their useless, frantic leaping—be repeatedly torn to pieces. (23)
Prahasta: As the Great King commands.
(Thus he exits. (A great clamor offstage; everyone listens with agitation. (Again, offstage:)
The preeminent elephant-warriors are being slain by the lords of the monkeys with their terrifying forms; and the defensive galleries are being bound on every side with severed heads.

These [monkeys], blinded by rage, are attempting to break through from the outside, yet in an instant they are split apart in the middle; and the city gates are being shattered on every side by boulders hurled against them. (24)
Rāvaṇa:

(Looking upward and rising in anger) How is it that even these denizens of heaven, led by Indra, lacking self-knowledge due to their partiality for the ascetics, are being agitated by my resentment? Therefore, O Queen, enter within. As for me, with some of my arms I shall scatter the intoxicated leaders of the monkeys in all directions, and with others, I shall crush those two young ascetics who act as actors in the performance of a mock battle.

Having plowed my own mind with the teachings of the cultured, I shall fill my own prison with those wicked denizens of heaven who have entered through the mere openings of my vain reflections, devoid as I am of compassion for them. (25)
(Thus, having walked about in a majestic manner, he exits.

(Then enters Vāsava with his retinue in a chariot, and the charioteer. Mātali: O Lord, Master of Heaven! Just as this [chariot] approaches Laṅkā, it is as fierce as the agitation caused by the collision of the waves of the seven lords of waters, which manifest their dissolution at the end of an aeon.
A tumultuous roar resounds intensely from the blood of thousands who are leaping about with violent movements of coming and going.
Thus I conjecture that the emperor of night-stalkers intends to go forth with a desire for battle.

Vāsava: Charioteer, look, look! Having observed this even more determined assault, the leader of the Rākṣasas, together with thousands of Rākṣasa guards—including his sons, kinsmen, and servants—has suddenly emerged from the city, having opened it with great impetuosity and put all the forest-dwellers to flight. (27)
(Miming the hearing of a sound: Ah! Who is this who approaches so impetuously from the northern quarter in a celestial chariot garlanded with a network of tinkling golden bells?
Sūta:
(Gazing) My Lord, Citraratha has been shown a great favor by you alone through the consecration to the sovereignty of the Gandharva kingdom.
(Then enters Citraratha, mounted upon his celestial chariot.
Citraratha: Victory, victory to the King of the Gods!
Vāsava: O King of the Gandharvas, why is your heart so filled with a desire to witness the battle?
Citraratha: That too.
Vāsava: What else?
Citraratha; the command of the Lord of Alakā.
Vāsava: Of what nature is he?
Citraratha: From the day of my birth, a certain most powerful and insurmountable affliction has grown within me, perhaps even more potent than that of the three worlds.
By the play of fate, this day of his death has arrived; may its outcome be auspicious, or otherwise. (28)
I have been sent to learn that.
Vāsava: This is the desire even of my kinsmen.

Citraratha: What is so wonderful about that? It is said that those natural enemies are mutually opposed. Furthermore, the wickedness of this villain, manifested through his conduct of seizing the treasure, the Puṣpaka chariot, and other things, is already well-known.

Or rather—indeed, as long as there exists any living being within the three worlds, all of them, having been tormented by his arrogant and evil deeds, await his defeat out of affection for the illustrious descendant of Raghu. (29)
Vāsava:

(Observing) O King of the Gandharvas, since this host of monkeys has suddenly rushed forth from the plateau of Mount Suvela, filling the directions with a powerful clamor of "kila-kila" shouts, I believe they have already fallen by the weapons.
Citraratha: O King of the Gods, look, look!
Here is the Lord of the Rākṣasas, standing in a chariot as elevated as the crest of a mountain, leading the way for those whose minds are skilled in the delights of battle;
with the repeated sounds of his bowstring, amplified by echoes from the distant peaks at the ends of the quarters, he deafens the entire expanse of the sky on all sides. (30)
Vāsava: O King of the Gandharvas, the preparations appropriate for the code of heroes have not yet been weighed against these two.
(With agitation) Charioteer, charioteer! Bring my battle-chariot for the noble Rāma; I, for my part, shall mount the celestial chariot presided over by the King of the Gandharvas.
(He does so accordingly.
Charioteer: As the King of the Gods commands.
(Thus he exits.
Citraratha: O King of the Gods, how chaotic is this battle, impossible to discern! For indeed:

the forest-dwelling lords have been driven from their positions by the Rākṣasas, who have lost all sense of order; they grapple hand-to-hand and hair-to-hair, their minds bewildered as they hurl their weapons at one another.

The battle commenced, so difficult to withstand that the bodies of the mutually crushing combatants were shattered; the path became impassable solely due to the streams of blood spouted forth from them. //31//
Moreover:

This is some extraordinary, ancient heap on the field of battle, resembling Citrakūṭa, which has grown from the massive, swelling bodies of adversaries hurled about by the operations of the broad, powerful arms of heroes—arms so skillful at cleaving apart headless trunks (ruṇḍa); there, millions of heroic "insects," rendered helpless by falling upon it, dissolve away. (32)

Vāsava: O King of the Gandharvas, this way, this way! On the outskirts of the battlefield, the steadfast warriors—having ceased their exertion, their bodies entirely smeared with the gushing blood from the weight of wounds inflicted by weapons—rest for half a moment. The heat is warded off by the shadow of the incomparable plumage of the king of vultures, who rushes about, eager to devour the cheeks of the fierce heroes stained with blood as they are transfixed by spears. (33)
For this reason as well:
the steadfast ones, maintaining their resolute composure, impetuously receive with their chests the weapons hurled at them by their enemies;
though the mass of their skin is torn away, their flesh crushed, their vessels, trunks, bones, and sinews severed, and the collection of their entrails clearly visible, they remain firm. (34)
Citraratha: O King of the Gods, unprecedented is this manifestation of the Lord of Rākṣasas as he enters the field of battle. For instance:

Meghanāda, surrounded by hundreds of younger brothers, stands at the boundary of the fray; Kumbhakarṇa, awakened and possessed of most formidable pride, is on the left flank along with other great heroes.

Even this extremely formidable host of Kaikeyī’s kinsmen, standing behind her, occupies the middle ground; seated upon the front of the chariot, he is as difficult to penetrate as the Vindhya mountains. //35//

Vāsava: O King of the Gandharvas, even upon beholding his enemy so intent on aggression, Rāmabhadra remains entirely unshaken. Or rather, this is only fitting; for: Even when a violent storm blows from every direction, those great mountain ranges, whose core substance is fully manifest, do not tremble in the slightest.
Nor do the oceans—their waters surging with the majesty of profound depth and their greatness immeasurable—ever abandon their boundaries. (36)
Citraratha: O King of the Gods, behold!

Having somehow released his younger brother—who was bowed low with devotion and whose sprout-like fingers were busily engaged in stringing his bow—for the sake of slaying Meghanāda, the bull among the Raghus once again consecrates the Lord of the Rākṣasas, who is skilled in battle and accompanied by his younger brothers, by making him the target of his arrows; he restores him to life through the touch of his grace. (37)
How is this? I consider it to be exceedingly difficult; for thus:
these millions of night-stalking warriors, having assailed one by one, simultaneously discharge showers of weapons from all sides to shroud the sprout of the radiant lineage.
Or rather, what indeed is difficult about this?

These two, whose majesty and power were augmented by their extraordinary prowess, engaged in battle on the field of war with an application of arrows made manifest by the fruit of shattering the weapons of their enemies. (38)

(Looking all around) Oh! How is it that even these forest-dwellers, in the midst of this great encounter with a host of enemies, merely explain the literal meaning of their own names? Only five or six attend at the feet of the noble Rāma. For instance:
Sugrīva is at the front of the chariot; behind him are those with Aṅgada;
five or six more are there; and Jāmbavān, who is to become the lord of Laṅkā, is on both sides. (39)

(Reflecting) Hanumān [approaches] the younger descendant of Kakutstha again. (With deliberation) It would be better if these very ones were to serve the lotus-feet of the illustrious Rāma in both ways; for by this, their devotion to their master, their fortitude, and their uninjured bodies will all be demonstrated.
But for others, the assault of Rākṣasas is seen, as well as extreme wretchedness.
Vāsava: O King of the Gandharvas, in the world of men, there exists a thing called "affection" (*vātsalya*), which is nothing other than a handful of powder that subjugates all the senses. For:
The son of Sumitrā is not inferior in any qualities, such as manual dexterity and the like; yet the son of Rāvaṇa is renowned for his essential greatness through the heat of his valor.

Thus, in this encounter where the two are indeed almost equal, while the rain of arrows from Rāma and the Lord of the Rākṣasas turns against one another, their affectionate gaze flows toward each other. (41)
Citraratha: O King of the Gods, this is indeed fitting; for it is said that great souls such as these are devoted to such affection. (With wonder and eagerness) Let the King of the Gods behold:
pierced more deeply by the thunderbolt-arrows of Saumitri’s shafts, these night-stalkers lie upon the battlefield like mountains, fleeing with their vital organs struck.
The Lord of the Rākṣasas, too, seeing several of his sons fallen and fearing the undesirable, abandons his assault on Rāma and rushes swiftly toward Meghanāda. //42//
I fear this is a great calamity.
Vāsava: O King of the Gandharvas, what indeed is this calamity? For these scions of the Kakutstha lineage are said to possess immeasurable majesty. To illustrate:
while thousands of lords of the night-stalkers were but a single target for this hero, even the Ten-necked one himself served as an ornament to the assembly of marvelous heroes in battles. (43)
Citraratha: O King of the Gods, even when one is attacked by many, the outcome is auspicious; this applies to the case of many individuals.
(With wonder) Let the King of the Gods attend to this:
As the Lord of the Rākṣasas has rushed out from here desiring battle, Kumbhakarṇa, pinned down by the arrows of the Lord of the Raghus, is agitated intensely.
Even Kumbha, beholding this state of his father who had come before him, wondered: "Is it Pride personified that has fallen, or is it a mountain-king moving swiftly on foot?"
(With astonishment: Oh, how the monkey species moves through openings! For:
A certain monkey intercepted in mid-air that proud elephant, the very first sprout of Daśaratha’s lineage, as it was falling from afar toward him on the battlefield.
(Observing more closely: How is this? Is it Sugrīva himself?
(With hesitation:
Then, having violently crushed him with his two arms and flung him to the ground, he stepped upon him—who was helpless under the sway of rage—and ground him to powder like a bean. //45//
Seeing this with apprehension, Kumbhakarṇa pounced and seized Sugrīva with a most fierce speed; but he too,
being skillful, released himself and simultaneously cut off both his [Kumbhakarṇa’s] nose and his own sister’s shame.
Vāsava! King of the Gandharvas, this way, this way!
This son of Raghu, though young, acted toward the lord of the Rākṣasas and the prince Meghanāda in such a wondrous manner that they instantly abandoned their blindness of rage. 47.
Ahaha! An exceedingly difficult task has fallen upon this child of Raghu.
For instance:

by the power of his mantras, he shook off the impenetrable serpent-nooses—whose course was otherwise difficult to perceive and which had been hurled by Meghanāda—through the employment of the weapon of the Lord of Birds.
Then, the leader of the Rākṣasas was again violently pierced in a vital spot by the enraged Hanumān with a śataghnī weapon; struck down by the blow, he fell instantly, deprived of consciousness.

Citraratha: O King of the Gods, this conflict here is even more wonderful. For when he perceived his brother’s delusion and—despite being the future Lord of Laṅkā—his mental state was suddenly permeated by the sentiment of compassionate heroism (*karuṇavīra*), and he was thus eager for a sight of him [Rāma], he was surrounded by the army of Rākṣasas led by Kumbhakarṇa; yet at that moment, he acted in this very manner. To illustrate: having assumed with his body that same disposition which the Conqueror of Cities formerly adopted during the victory over Tripura, this Bull among the Raghus...
In an instant, having torn the army of the Lord of Rākṣasas into pieces with his arrows and reduced it to ashes, he rushes toward his younger brother with the utmost eagerness.
(Gazing intently) Oh, the greatness of the affection of the bull among the Raghus, by which he recognized the condition of his younger brother the very moment it was made an object of his perception!

(Looking all around; with joy) By good fortune, I perceive that all is well with these two princes of the Raghu clan, since even the lord of the Rākṣasas, along with his entire retinue, has been thrown into confusion by the slaying of Kumbhakarṇa during this great ocean of calamity for them.
(Gazing at the two again) How is it that they are still as if unconscious? A most grievous misfortune has indeed befallen them; for:
The Rākṣasas are full of many deceits, and the two enemies are themselves superior;
such is the situation, and even those monkeys who are your allies are disheartened. (50)
Therefore, I do not know what kind of preliminary action or divine intervention is required in this matter.

Vāsava: O King of the Gandharvas, why do you entertain such apprehension? Behold! This son of the Wind-god (Hanumān), whose vast majesty is of inconceivable extent, has indeed been awakened by Jāmbavat. Now, with his hair standing on end, imitating a rain of dust swirling at the time of universal dissolution, his incomparable tail—its tip slightly curved—having cast aside the circle of stars through its whirling motion, this wise one, having leaped excessively with a resolve matching his great eagerness, has returned in half a moment carrying some mountain peak from somewhere unknown. (51)
Citraratha:
(Reflecting; with joy) O King of the Gods, look, look!
Just as the mass of night-lotuses [longs for] the moonlight, as the essence of stone [longs for] a magnet, so too does the ocean of worldly existence long for you, even though you have entered it.
Having thus reflected, these two suddenly burst forth upon seeing the mountain brought by Hanumān; indeed, the greatness of a thing is something profound. //52//

(Looking toward the south: How is it that this Lord of Laṅkā, drawing forth the Rākṣasa host like the ocean’s tide at the end of an aeon, advances once more against the enemy? (Reflecting: But now there is the prospect of a righteous war; for when the majority of the principal figures have been struck down, this entire Rākṣasa army—consisting of nothing but Rāvaṇa and Meghanāda—is no longer even counted, let alone these two, much less the thousands of other mere insects among warriors.

(Looking at Lakṣmaṇa again: This descendant of Raghu shines loftily like a sun released from a thick cloud after being polished on a whetstone, like a sword drawn from its scabbard, or like the lord of serpents suddenly shedding his slough.
What indeed could it be? Or what else? It is some divine herb; a certain majesty of inconceivable power triumphs. (53)
(Observing: How is it that the combat between the two warriors who serve at the vanguard of the monkey and the Rākṣasa has already begun once more? For instance:

With sharp arrows, some on the field of battle, and others with their keen claws, their minds seized by a competitive spirit of "I first, you second" (*ahamahamikā*) due to the continuous flow of action, they pierced one another, their broad chests fragrant from the *piṣṭātaka* powder [of crushed flowers] mixed with the dust of the earth shattered by the intense friction of their powerful collision. (54)

(Reflecting with particular certainty: The interval between these two forces is like that between the approaching morning twilight and the deep darkness or the first glimmer of dawn. For instance: at every moment this army of Rākṣasas is wasting away even more, while the host of monkeys increases by infinitely greater degrees. (55)
Vāsava: O King of the Gandharvas, a great slaughter has once again begun here.

The Lord of the Rākṣasas and the son of Raghu, the son of Rāvaṇa and Lakṣmaṇa, having swiftly entered into single combat with the sovereign of the earth—both displaying the majesty of their exultant arm-strength and their training in the bow—they engaged in the employment of divine weapons and performed fitting counter-moves against one another; they rendered each other unconscious, surpassing even the conflagration at the end of an aeon, and brought ruin upon their respective armies. (56)
Citraratha: O King of the Gods, this mutual clash between these two great heroes is difficult to comprehend. For instance:

While they both long shroud the quarters with their war-cries, the sky with their masses of arrows, and the surface of the earth with the bodies of their enemies torn in two, they cause the bodies of us who watch them to become blurred by tears, repeatedly filled with sudden horripilation and trembling. (57)
(Reflecting with particular care: How is it that a single reality, perceived through both direct perception and inference, becomes so vastly different? For instance:
I behold the deeds of Rāghava as being ten times greater than these deeds of Rāvaṇa; yet I infer them to be infinitely greater by the way the lords of the demons fell at his side. (58)
(Looking all around; with curiosity and wonder:

As many night-rangers as there were—those whose arms were raised in brandishing weapons, who rushed forward to fight face-to-face, and who were puffed up with the pride of their throbbing arms—all of them, upon entering the fire of Rāma’s prowess, which was fanned by the wind from the feathers of his discharged arrows, wondrously turned into moths in an instant. (59)

(Reflecting) Such indeed is this creation composed of the five elements! Even the three worlds would not have been sufficient for these Rākṣasas to dwell in, yet they have simply dissolved upon the earth, having met their destruction. (60)
Vāsava: O King of the Gandharvas, behold these two—Rāvaṇa and Rāvaṇī—who are truly a source of wonder and deception! For:

While the heads of one are being severed with interest by the arrows of these two descendants of Raghu, even a single head of the other remains as if infinite; how much more so for the second, whose qualities are equal?

Even as they watch this for a very long time, some inconceivable power prevails such that neither their enthusiasm nor their fortitude ceases, nor does the flight of the feathered arrows from the cutting of the heads. (61)

(Offstage: O Rāmabhadra, why do you still neglect this wicked one? And how can such a vast objective be accomplished by a single action? Listen for a moment: You shall have Sītā; the world throughout the three realms shall have its fitting joy; the younger son of Pulastya [Rāvaṇa] shall regain his own city and immortality. What else is there? May the host of sages, having realized the supreme reality, attain peace in their minds as their joy blossoms through your grace. (62)
Citraratha:
(Listening) What! Even this host of divine sages is urging the two Raghavas to slay these two? Or rather, for whom would the pacification of the wicked not bring joy to the heart?
(With agitation, wonder, and eagerness) O King of the Gods, look!
By these two descendants of Raghu, with arrows fragrant from the recollection of the infallible weapons of Brahmā, the heads of Rāvaṇa, the lord of the night-stalkers, were severed in succession.

Afterwards, that demon Kabandha fell helpless upon the earth in the field of battle, and a rain of flowers fell from the sky upon the heads of the two illustrious sons of Daśaratha and upon the earth.

Vāsava: (Looking toward the tiring-room; with joy) O King of the Gandharvas, look! These very gods, filled with joy upon hearing the news of the destruction of the ten-headed one—the enemy of the three worlds—along with the great sages, are waiting for me alone, desiring to partake in some great festival. Therefore, I shall go to fulfill their heart's desire. You too, by reporting this event, please my dear friend, the Lord of Alakā.
(Thus, having walked around, they all exit.
//The Sixth Act//
